title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 2, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 13–14 (Night 226, continuing nights-225), transcribed from the scan (archive.org aliflailaorbook02unkngoog) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 226 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Taking the road through the middle of the mountain, al-Amjad and al-Asʿad walk all day and into the night until al-Asʿad collapses, and al-Amjad carries him by turns until dawn. On the summit they find a spring, a pomegranate tree and a little oratory, and rest there three days while al-Asʿad's swollen feet recover; then, after more days and nights of thirst on the heights, a city comes into view. Al-Asʿad insists that he, not his brother, go down to it, and in its lanes he meets a richly dressed old man with a great red turban and a beard parted in two, who asks whether he is a stranger — and morning overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّادِسَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sādisatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾatayni
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the sixth and the twenty after the two-hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the two hundred and twenty-sixth night,
sentences.n: The print has اليلة, a misprint for الليلة, corrected here. The night's opening formula: the unit, al-sādisatu, comes before the tens and is joined to them by wa-, all in the nominative with al-laylatu. The ئ of المائتين is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْأَمْجَدَ وَالْأَسْعَدَ أَوْلَادَ الْمَلِكِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا عَادَا مِنَ الطَّرِيقِ الصَّاعِدَةِ فِى الْجَبَلِ إِلَى الطَّرِيقِ الْمَسْلُوكَةِ فِي وَسَطِهِ مَشَيَا فِيهَا طُولَ ذٰلِكَ النَّهَارِ إِلَي اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-Amjada wa-al-Asʿada awlāda al-maliki Qamari al-Zamāni lammā ʿādā mina al-ṭarīqi al-ṣāʿidati fī al-jabali ilā al-ṭarīqi al-maslūkati fī wasaṭihi mashayā fīhā ṭūla dhālika al-nahāri ilā al-layli
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that al-Amjad and-al-Asʿad, (the) children (of) King Qamar al-Zamān, when they-two-returned from the-road climbing in the-mountain to the-road travelled in its-middle, they-two-walked on-it (the) length (of) that day until the-night.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when al-Amjad and al-Asʿad, the sons of King Qamar al-Zamān, had come back from the road that climbed the mountain to the beaten road through its middle, they walked along it all that day until nightfall.
sentences.n: awlāda, “children, sons”, is a plural used of the two brothers, where Classical Arabic would say waladay, the dual; it stands in apposition to al-Amjada wa-al-Asʿada, the accusative noun of anna. The predicate of anna is the whole clause lammā ʿādā … mashayā, “when they had returned … they walked”. ʿāda min … ilā, “to return from … to”: min marks the road left, ilā the road reached. ṭarīq is feminine here, as in the night before: al-ṣāʿidati, al-maslūkati and fīhā all agree with it. maslūk, passive participle of salaka, “gone along”, so “the travelled road, the beaten track”. ṭūla al-nahāri, “the length of the day”, an adverbial accusative of time. The print spells fī once with ى, فى, and the second ilā with ي, الي; both are kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ تَعِبَ الْأَسْعَدُ مِنْ كَثْرَةِ السَّيْرِ فَقَالَ لِأَخِيهِ يَا أَخِي أَنَا مَا بَقِيتُ أَقْدِرُ عَلَى الْمَشْيِ فَإِنِّي ضَعُفْتُ جِدًّا
sentences.tr: wa-qad taʿiba al-Asʿadu min kathrati al-sayri fa-qāla li-akhīhi yā akhī anā mā baqītu aqdiru ʿalā al-mashyi fa-innī ḍaʿuftu jiddan
sentences.l: And-al-Asʿad had grown-tired from (the) muchness (of) the-going, and-he-said to-his-brother: O my-brother, I, not I-remained I-am-able for the-walking, for-indeed-I I-have-grown-weak very.
sentences.i: Al-Asʿad was worn out with so much travelling, and he said to his brother, “O my brother, I can walk no further, for I have grown very weak.”
sentences.n: min kathrati al-sayri, “from the much travelling”: min of cause. mā baqītu aqdiru, “I no longer can”, literally “I did not remain able”: baqiya with an imperfect and a negative is the spoken way of saying “no longer”. qadara ʿalā, “to be able for”: ʿalā marks what one can do. ḍaʿufa, “to grow weak”; its damma on the ت, ضعفتُ, and the tanwīn and shadda of جدًّا, are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْأَمْجَدُ يَا أَخِي مُدَّ رُوحَكَ لَعَلَّ اللّٰهَ يُفَرِّجُ عَنَّا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-Amjadu yā akhī mudda rūḥaka laʿalla Allāha yufarriju ʿannā
sentences.l: And-said to-him al-Amjad: O my-brother, stretch your-soul; perhaps God relieves from-us.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said to him, “O my brother, bear up a little longer; it may be that God will bring us relief.”
sentences.n: mudda rūḥaka, “stretch out your soul”, is not Classical; it seems to be a spoken idiom for “have patience, hold out”, like the more familiar ṭawwil rūḥak, and is translated so, with that doubt admitted. rūḥ, “soul, breath”, stands for the self, as often in the later language. farraja ʿan, Form II of f-r-j, “to relieve, take trouble away from”: ʿan marks those set free. The shadda of مدّ, لعلّ, يفرّج and عنّا is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا مَشَيَا سَاعَةً مِنَ اللَّيْلِ وَقَدْ أَظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمَا الظَّلَامُ وَتَعِبَ الْأَسْعَدُ تَعَبًا شَدِيدًا مَا عَلَيْهِ مِنْ مَزِيدٍ
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā mashayā sāʿatan mina al-layli wa-qad aẓlama ʿalayhimā al-ẓalāmu wa-taʿiba al-Asʿadu taʿaban shadīdan mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin
sentences.l: Then indeed-they-two walked an-hour of the-night, and-had grown-dark over-them-two the-darkness, and-al-Asʿad tired a-tiring severe, not upon-it of increase.
sentences.i: Then they walked on for part of the night, and the darkness closed in upon them, and al-Asʿad grew tired with a weariness that could not be greater.
sentences.n: thumma innahumā, “then they”: the storyteller often restarts a sentence with inna after thumma. sāʿa, “hour”, is any stretch of time, not sixty minutes. aẓlama ʿalayhimā al-ẓalāmu, “the darkness grew dark over them”, a jingle of verb and noun from the same root. taʿiba taʿaban shadīdan, “he tired a severe tiring”, the verbal noun used as an object to intensify the verb; mā ʿalayhi min mazīdin, “there is no increase upon it”, a stock phrase for “beyond measure”: min before an indefinite noun after a negative means “any”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ يَا أَخِي إِنِّي تَعِبْتُ وَكَلَّيْتُ مِنَ الْمَشْيِ وَرَمَى نَفْسَهُ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ وَبَكَى
sentences.tr: wa-qāla yā akhī innī taʿibtu wa-kallaytu mina al-mashyi wa-ramā nafsahu ʿalā al-arḍi wa-bakā
sentences.l: And-he-said: O my-brother, indeed-I I-have-tired and-I-have-wearied from the-walking. And-he-threw himself on the-ground and-wept.
sentences.i: And he said, “O my brother, I am tired and worn out with walking,” and he threw himself on the ground and wept.
sentences.n: kallaytu, “I am weary”, is a Middle Arabic form: kalla, “to be weary”, is a doubled verb whose Classical first person is kalaltu, but the later language conjugates such verbs like those ending in a weak letter, with -aytu. Its shadda and the damma on the ت, كلّيتُ, are printed, as is the damma of تعبتُ. ramā nafsahu, “he threw himself”: nafs with a suffix is the reflexive “self”.

sentences.t: فَحَمَلَهُ أَخُوهُ الْأَمْجَدُ وَمَشَى بِهِ وَصَارَ سَاعَةً يَحْمِلُهُ وَيَمْشِي وَسَاعَةً يَقْعُدُ وَ يَسْتَرِيحُ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَ الصَّبَاحُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥamalahu akhūhu al-Amjadu wa-mashā bihi wa-ṣāra sāʿatan yaḥmiluhu wa-yamshī wa-sāʿatan yaqʿudu wa-yastarīḥu ilā an ṭalaʿa al-ṣabāḥu
sentences.l: So-carried-him his-brother al-Amjad, and-walked with-him, and-began, an-hour he-carries-him and-walks, and-an-hour he-sits and-rests, until that rose the-morning.
sentences.i: So his brother al-Amjad took him up and walked on carrying him, now bearing him along, now sitting down to rest, until the morning broke.
sentences.n: mashā bihi, “he walked with him”: bi- here marks what is carried along, so “walked carrying him”. ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to, kept on”. sāʿatan … wa-sāʿatan, “one while … and another while”, adverbial accusatives. ilā an ṭalaʿa, “until it rose”: ilā an with a perfect means “until”. The print sets wa- by itself at the end of a line, و, and begins the next with يستريح; the two are kept apart as printed and read together, wa-yastarīḥu.

sentences.t: فَطَلَعَ هُوَ وَإِيَّاهُ فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ فَوَجَدَا عَيْنَ مَاءٍ يَجْرِي وَعِنْدَهَا شَجَرَةُ رُمَّانٍ وَمِحْرَابٌ
sentences.tr: fa-ṭalaʿa huwa wa-iyyāhu fawqa al-jabali fa-wajadā ʿayna māʾin yajrī wa-ʿindahā shajaratu rummānin wa-miḥrābun
sentences.l: And-climbed he and-him up the-mountain, and-they-two-found a-spring (of) water running, and-by-it a-tree (of) pomegranate and-a-prayer-niche.
sentences.i: Then he and his brother climbed to the top of the mountain, and there they found a spring of running water, with a pomegranate tree beside it and a prayer-niche.
sentences.n: huwa wa-iyyāhu, “he and him”, is the spoken way of saying “he and the other”: iyyāhu, properly an object pronoun, is joined to the subject as a second subject, where Classical Arabic would name the other, huwa wa-akhūhu, or put the verb in the dual. The verb stays singular, ṭalaʿa, with the first subject, and only the next, wajadā, is dual. ṭalaʿa, “to come up, climb”; fawqa al-jabali, “on top of the mountain”. ʿayn, “spring”, is feminine, as ʿindahā, “by it”, shows, but yajrī, “running”, is masculine: either it goes with māʾ, “water”, or the text lets ʿayn be masculine, as the spoken language may. miḥrāb is the niche in a mosque that shows the direction of prayer; here it seems to be a small place of prayer built in the wild, a hermit's oratory. The shadda of رمّان is printed.

sentences.t: فَمَا صَدَّقَا أَنَّهُمَا يَرَيَانِ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-mā ṣaddaqā annahumā yarayāni dhālika
sentences.l: And-not they-two-believed that-they-two see that.
sentences.i: They could scarcely believe that they were seeing it.
sentences.n: mā ṣaddaqā, “they did not believe”: ṣaddaqa, Form II, “to believe, hold true”, with the negative is the later language's phrase for joy at something too good to be true. yarayāni, the dual imperfect of raʾā, “to see”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسَا عِنْدَ تِلْكَ الْعَيْنِ وَشَرِبَا مِنْ مَائِهَا وَأَكَلَا مِنْ رُمَّانِ تِلْكَ الشَّجَرَةِ وَنَامَا فِي ذٰلِكَ الْمَوْضِعِ حَتَّى طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ
sentences.tr: thumma jalasā ʿinda tilka al-ʿayni wa-sharibā min māʾihā wa-akalā min rummāni tilka al-shajarati wa-nāmā fī dhālika al-mawḍiʿi ḥattā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu
sentences.l: Then they-two-sat by that the-spring, and-drank from its-water, and-ate from (the) pomegranates (of) that the-tree, and-slept in that the-place until rose the-sun.
sentences.i: Then they sat down by the spring, drank of its water and ate of the pomegranates of the tree, and slept in that place until the sun was up.
sentences.n: shariba min and akala min: min marks the partitive, “some of”. rummān is a collective, “pomegranates”. The ئ of مائها and the shadda of رمّان are printed.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَا وَاغْتَسَلَا فِي الْعَيْنِ وَأَكَلَا مِنْ ذٰلِكَ الرُّمَّانِ الَّذِي فِى الشَّجَرَةِ وَنَامَا إِلَى الْعَصْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasā wa-ightasalā fī al-ʿayni wa-akalā min dhālika al-rummāni alladhī fī al-shajarati wa-nāmā ilā al-ʿaṣri
sentences.l: And-they-two-sat-up and-washed-themselves in the-spring, and-ate from that the-pomegranate which (is) on the-tree, and-slept until the-afternoon.
sentences.i: Then they sat up and bathed in the spring, and ate of those pomegranates on the tree, and slept until the afternoon.
sentences.n: ightasala, Form VIII of gh-s-l, “to wash oneself, bathe”. ʿaṣr, “afternoon”, the time of the afternoon prayer. The print spells fī here with ى, فى.

sentences.t: وَأَرَادَا أَنْ يَسِيرَا فَمَا قَدَرَ الْأَسْعَدُ أَنْ يَسِيرَ وَقَدْ وَرِمَتْ رِجْلَاهُ
sentences.tr: wa-arādā an yasīrā fa-mā qadara al-Asʿadu an yasīra wa-qad warimat rijlāhu
sentences.l: And-they-two-wanted that they-two-go, but-not was-able al-Asʿad that he-go, and-had swollen his-two-feet.
sentences.i: They meant to go on, but al-Asʿad could not walk, for his feet had swollen.
sentences.n: an yasīrā, “that they go”, the subjunctive dual after an. qadara an, “to be able to”. wa-qad warimat rijlāhu, “his feet having swollen”, a circumstantial clause with qad giving the reason. rijlāhu, “his two feet”, the dual of rijl in the nominative, with the n dropped before the suffix; the verb warimat is feminine because rijl is.

sentences.t: فَأَقَامَا هُنَاكَ ثَلٰثَةَ أَيَّامٍ حَتَّى اسْتَرَاحَا
sentences.tr: fa-aqāmā hunāka thalāthata ayyāmin ḥattā istarāḥā
sentences.l: So-they-two-stayed there three days until they-two-rested.
sentences.i: So they stayed there three days, until they had rested.
sentences.n: aqāma, Form IV of q-w-m, “to stay, remain”. thalāthata ayyāmin: a numeral from three to ten takes the feminine form with a masculine noun, and the counted noun follows in the genitive plural. The print spells thalātha with a small dagger alif, ثلٰثة, rather than a full alif.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَارَا فِي الْجَبَلِ مُدَّةَ أَيَّامٍ وَلَيَالِي وَهُمَا سَائِرَانِ فَوْقَ الْجَبَلِ وَقَدْ هَلَكَا وَتَعِبَا مِنَ الْعَطَشِ إِلَى أَنْ لَاحَتْ لَهُمَا مَدِينَةٌ مِنْ بَعِيدٍ
sentences.tr: thumma sārā fī al-jabali muddata ayyāmin wa-layālī wa-humā sāʾirāni fawqa al-jabali wa-qad halakā wa-taʿibā mina al-ʿaṭashi ilā an lāḥat lahumā madīnatun min baʿīdin
sentences.l: Then they-two-went in the-mountain (the) span (of) days and-nights, and-they-two (were) going over the-mountain, and-had perished and-tired from the-thirst, until that appeared to-them-two a-city from afar.
sentences.i: Then they travelled through the mountains for some days and nights, journeying over the heights, near to death and worn out with thirst, until at last a city came into view far off.
sentences.n: muddata ayyāmin wa-layālī, “for a space of days and nights”, an adverbial accusative. layālī keeps its final ي where Classical grammar, in this genitive, has layālin; it is a Middle Arabic form. wa-humā sāʾirāni, “while they were going”, a circumstantial clause; the ئ of سائران is printed. halakā, “they perished”, here by exaggeration “they were near death”; min al-ʿaṭashi, “from thirst”: min of cause. lāḥa li-, “to appear to, gleam before”: li- marks the ones who see it. min baʿīdin, “from afar”.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَا وَسَافَرَا حَتَّى وَصَلَا إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥā wa-sāfarā ḥattā waṣalā ilayhā
sentences.l: And-they-two-rejoiced and-travelled until they-two-arrived at-it.
sentences.i: They were glad, and journeyed on until they reached it.
sentences.n: waṣala ilā, “to arrive at”: ilā marks the place reached.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرُبَا مِنْهَا شَكَرَا لِلّٰهِ تَعَالَى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qarubā minhā shakarā li-Allāhi taʿālā
sentences.l: And-when they-two-drew-near from-it, they-two-thanked to-God, (may) He-be-exalted.
sentences.i: When they drew near it, they gave thanks to God the Exalted.
sentences.n: qaruba min, “to come near to”: min marks what is approached. shakara li-, “to thank”: Classical Arabic says either shakarahu or shakara lahu, and li- marks the one thanked. taʿālā, “may He be exalted”, follows the name of God.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَمْجَدُ لِلْأَسْعَدِ يَا أَخِي اجْلِسْ هُنَا وَأَنَا أَمْضِي وَأَسِيرُ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَأَنْظُرُ مَا هِيَ وَلِمَنْ هِيَ وَأَيْنَ نَحْنُ مِنْ أَرْضِ اللّٰهِ الْوَاسِعَةِ وَنَعْرِفُ الَّذِي قَطَعْنَاهُ مِنَ الْبِلَادِ فِي عَرْضِ هٰذَا الْجَبَلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-Amjadu li-al-Asʿadi yā akhī ijlis hunā wa-anā amḍī wa-asīru ilā hādhihi al-madīnati wa-anẓuru mā hiya wa-li-man hiya wa-ayna naḥnu min arḍi Allāhi al-wāsiʿati wa-naʿrifu alladhī qaṭaʿnāhu mina al-bilādi fī ʿarḍi hādhā al-jabali
sentences.l: And-said al-Amjad to-al-Asʿad: O my-brother, sit here, and-I go-off and-make-my-way to this the-city, and-see what (is) it, and-to-whom (is) it, and-where (are) we of (the) land (of) God, the-wide; and-we-know that-which we-have-crossed-it of the-countries in (the) breadth (of) this the-mountain.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said to al-Asʿad, “O my brother, sit here, and I will go down to this city and see what city it is and whose it is, and where we are in God's wide earth, and we shall know how much country we have crossed over the breadth of this mountain.
sentences.n: wa-anā amḍī, “and I will go”: the imperfect after a command carries a future sense, and the pronoun anā sets the speaker against the brother who stays. maḍā, “to go off, go away”. naẓara mā hiya, “to see what it is”; li-man hiya, “whose is it”: li- marks the owner. ayna naḥnu min arḍi Allāhi, “where we are in God's earth”: min marks the whole in which they are placed. qaṭaʿa, “to cut”, also “to cross, traverse” a distance; alladhī qaṭaʿnāhu, “that which we have crossed it”: the relative is taken up by -hu inside its clause, and min al-bilādi says what it was, “of country”. ʿarḍ, “breadth”.

sentences.t: وَلَوْ أَنَّنَا مَشَيْنَا فِي لِحْفِهِ مَا كُنَّا نَصِلُ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَهِ فِي سَنَةٍ كَامِلَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-law annanā mashaynā fī liḥfihi mā kunnā naṣilu ilā hādhihi al-madīnati fī sanatin kāmilatin
sentences.l: And-if that-we had-walked in its-foot, not we-were we-reach to this the-city in a-year complete.
sentences.i: Had we gone along its foot, we would not have reached this city in a whole year.
sentences.n: law annanā, “if it were that we”: law takes anna before a clause, and its answer here has no la-, mā kunnā naṣilu, “we would not have been reaching”. kāna with an imperfect makes a past of what would have gone on. liḥf, “foot, lower slope of a mountain”: the road that climbs over the mountain has been a short cut. The kasra of لِحفه and the shadda of انّنا are printed. madīna is spelled here with ه for ة, المدينه, as the print does now and then; it is kept and read as al-madīnati.

sentences.t: فَالْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ عَلَى السَّلَامَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi ʿalā al-salāmati
sentences.l: So-the-praise (is) to-God for the-safety.
sentences.i: Praise be to God that we are safe.”
sentences.n: al-ḥamdu li-Allāhi ʿalā, “praise be to God for”: li- marks the one to whom the praise belongs, ʿalā the thing it is given for. salāma, “safety, a safe arrival”, the word still said to a traveller who has come through.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْأَسْعَدُ وَاللّٰهِ يَا أَخِي مَا يَنْزِلُ وَيَذْهَبُ إِلَى هٰذِهِ الْمَدِينَةِ غَيْرِي وَأَنَا فِدَاكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-Asʿadu wa-Allāhi yā akhī mā yanzilu wa-yadhhabu ilā hādhihi al-madīnati ghayrī wa-anā fidāka
sentences.l: And-said to-him al-Asʿad: By-God, O my-brother, not goes-down and-goes to this the-city other-than-me, and-I (am) your-ransom.
sentences.i: Al-Asʿad said to him, “By God, my brother, no one shall go down to this city but me — may I be your ransom!
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of the oath, governing the genitive. mā yanzilu … ghayrī, “none goes down … but me”: ghayr, “other than”, stands as the subject at the end of its clause. anā fidāka, “I am your ransom”, a formula of devotion: the speaker offers himself in the other's place, and so takes the risk on himself.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّكَ إِنْ تَرَكْتَنِي وَنَزَلْتَ أَنْتَ السَّاعَةَ وَغِبْتَ عَنِّى حَسَبْتُ أَنَا أَلْفَ حِسَابٍ وَتَسْتَغْرِقُنِى الْأَفْكَارُ مِنْ أَجْلِكَ وَلَيْسَ لِي قُدْرَةٌ عَلَى بُعْدِكَ عَنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-innaka in taraktanī wa-nazalta anta al-sāʿata wa-ghibta ʿannī ḥasabtu anā alfa ḥisābin wa-tastaghriqunī al-afkāru min ajlika wa-laysa lī qudratun ʿalā buʿdika ʿannī
sentences.l: For-indeed-you, if you-leave-me and-go-down you the-hour and-are-absent from-me, I-reckon, I, a-thousand reckoning(s), and-engulf-me the-thoughts for your-sake; and-there-is-not for-me power for your-farness from-me.
sentences.i: For if you leave me and go down now and are gone from me, I shall be counting a thousand fears, and my thoughts will swallow me up for your sake; I cannot bear to have you far from me.”
sentences.n: in with perfects, taraktanī … ḥasabtu, “if you leave me … I shall reckon”: in a condition the perfect stands for the future. al-sāʿata, “at this hour, now”. ghāba ʿan, “to be absent from”: ʿan marks the one left behind; the fatḥa on the ت, غبتَ, is printed. ḥasabtu alfa ḥisābin, “I shall reckon a thousand reckonings”, a spoken phrase for imagining every danger; ḥisāb is the verbal noun of ḥasaba, “to count”. istaghraqa, Form X of gh-r-q, “to absorb, engulf”; tastaghriqunī is feminine singular to agree with the broken plural al-afkāru, “thoughts”. min ajlika, “for your sake”. qudra ʿalā, “ability to bear”: ʿalā marks what one can or cannot endure. The print spells ʿannī once with ى, عنّى, and once with ي, عنّي, and writes تستغرقنى with ى; all are kept. The shaddas of عنّى and عنّي are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْأَمْجَدُ انْزِلْ وَلَا تُبْطِئْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-Amjadu inzil wa-lā tubṭiʾ
sentences.l: And-said to-him al-Amjad: Go-down, and-do-not delay.
sentences.i: Al-Amjad said to him, “Go down, then, and do not be long.”
sentences.n: lā with the jussive, lā tubṭiʾ, is the negative command. abṭaʾa, Form IV of b-ṭ-ʾ, “to be slow, delay”; the ئ of تبطئ is printed.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَ الْأَسْعَدُ مِنَ الْجَبَلِ وَأَخَذَ مَعَهُ دَنَانِيرَ وَخَلَّى أَخَاهُ يَنْتَظِرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-nazala al-Asʿadu mina al-jabali wa-akhadha maʿahu danānīra wa-khallā akhāhu yantaẓiruhu
sentences.l: So-went-down al-Asʿad from the-mountain, and-took with-him dinars, and-left his-brother he-waits-for-him.
sentences.i: So al-Asʿad went down from the mountain, taking some dinars with him, and left his brother waiting for him.
sentences.n: danānīr, plural of dīnār, the gold coin, a diptote without tanwīn. khallā, Form II of kh-l-w, “to leave, let”, is the ordinary verb of the spoken language for “leave someone doing something”, followed by the imperfect yantaẓiruhu, “waiting for him”; Classical prose would say taraka. The print writes it with ى, خلى.

sentences.t: وَسَارَ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ مَاشِيًا فِى أَسْفَلِ الْجَبَلِ حَتَّى دَخَلَ الْمَدِينَةَ وَشَقَّ فِي أَزِقَّتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-sāra wa-lam yazal māshiyan fī asfali al-jabali ḥattā dakhala al-madīnata wa-shaqqa fī aziqqatihā
sentences.l: And-he-went, and-not he-ceased walking in (the) lower-part (of) the-mountain, until he-entered the-city and-cut-through in its-lanes.
sentences.i: Off he went, and kept walking along the foot of the mountain until he came into the city and made his way through its lanes.
sentences.n: lam yazal māshiyan, “he did not cease walking”, lam yazal with a participle in the accusative. asfal, “the lowest part”, an elative used as a noun. shaqqa fī, “to cut through, make one's way through”: fī marks the place passed through. aziqqa, plural of zuqāq, “lane, alley”. The shadda of شقّ and ازقّتها is printed, and the print spells fī here with ى, فى.

sentences.t: فَلَقِيَهُ فِي طَرِيقِهِ رَجُلٌ وَهُوَ شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ طَاعِنٌ فِى السِّنِّ وَقَدْ نَزَلَتْ لِحْيَتُهُ عَلَى صَدْرِهِ وَافْتَرَقَتْ فِرْقَتَيْنِ وَبِيَدِهِ عُكَّازٌ وَعَلَيْهِ ثِيَابٌ فَاخِرَةٌ وَعَلَى رَأْسِهِ عِمَامَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ حَمْرَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-laqiyahu fī ṭarīqihi rajulun wa-huwa shaykhun kabīrun ṭāʿinun fī al-sinni wa-qad nazalat liḥyatuhu ʿalā ṣadrihi wa-iftaraqat firqatayni wa-bi-yadihi ʿukkāzun wa-ʿalayhi thiyābun fākhiratun wa-ʿalā raʾsihi ʿimāmatun kabīratun ḥamrāʾu
sentences.l: And-met-him on his-way a-man, and-he (was) an-old-man great, advanced in the-age; and-had come-down his-beard upon his-chest and-parted (into) two-parts; and-in-his-hand a-staff, and-on-him clothes splendid, and-on his-head a-turban big red.
sentences.i: On his way he was met by a man, an old man, far gone in years, whose beard came down over his chest and parted in two; he had a staff in his hand, rich clothes upon him, and on his head a great red turban.
sentences.n: wa-huwa shaykhun, “and he an old man”, a circumstantial clause describing the man. ṭāʿin fī al-sinn, “advanced in age”, literally “piercing into age”: fī marks what he has gone far into. iftaraqat firqatayni, “it parted into two parts”: the accusative names what it divided into, as with the road in the night before. bi-yadihi, “in his hand”: bi- marks where a thing is held. ʿukkāz, “staff, walking stick”; its damma and shadda, عُكّاز, are printed. ʿimāma, “turban”; ḥamrāʾ, feminine of aḥmar, “red”, a diptote; its ء is printed, and the أ of رأسه.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهُ الْأَسْعَدُ تَعَجَّبَ مِنْ لِبْسِهِ وَزِيِّهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhu al-Asʿadu taʿajjaba min libsihi wa-ziyyihi
sentences.l: And-when saw-him al-Asʿad, he-wondered at his-clothing and-his-garb.
sentences.i: When al-Asʿad saw him he marvelled at his clothing and his garb.
sentences.n: taʿajjaba min, “to wonder at”: min marks what causes the wonder; its shadda, تعجّب, is printed. libs, “clothing”; ziyy, “dress, outward appearance, the costume that marks a man's rank”; its shadda, زيّه, is printed, as is the آ of رآه.

sentences.t: وَتَقَدَّمَ إِلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ أَيْنَ طَرِيقُ السُّوقِ يَا سَيِّدِي
sentences.tr: wa-taqaddama ilayhi wa-sallama ʿalayhi wa-qāla lahu ayna ṭarīqu al-sūqi yā sayyidī
sentences.l: And-he-stepped-forward to-him and-greeted upon-him, and-said to-him: Where (is the) road (of) the-market, O my-lord?
sentences.i: He went up to him and greeted him and said, “Which is the way to the market, my lord?”
sentences.n: The print has الصوق, a misprint for السوق, corrected here. taqaddama ilā, Form V of q-d-m, “to step up to”: ilā marks the one approached. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”, literally to say al-salāmu ʿalaykum over someone; ʿalā marks the one greeted, and the shadda of سلّم is printed. yā sayyidī, “my lord”, the polite address to an elder.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الشَّيْخُ كَلَامَهُ تَبَسَّمَ فِي وَجْهِهِ وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا وَلَدِي كَأَنَّكَ غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-shaykhu kalāmahu tabassama fī wajhihi wa-qāla lahu yā waladī kaʾannaka gharībun
sentences.l: And-when heard the-old-man his-speech, he-smiled in his-face and-said to-him: O my-son, as-if-you (are) a-stranger.
sentences.i: When the old man heard him speak, he smiled in his face and said, “My son, it seems you are a stranger here.”
sentences.n: tabassama fī wajhihi, “he smiled in his face”: fī marks the face the smile is turned to; the shadda of تبسّم is printed. kaʾannaka, “as though you”, ka- “like” joined to anna; it is the ordinary way to say “it looks as if”. gharīb, “stranger, one far from home”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْأَسْعَدُ نَعَمْ أَنَا غَرِيبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-Asʿadu naʿam anā gharībun
sentences.l: And-said to-him al-Asʿad: Yes, I (am) a-stranger.
sentences.i: “Yes,” said al-Asʿad, “I am a stranger.”
sentences.n: anā gharībun, “I am a stranger”, a sentence without a verb: Arabic has no present “to be”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night. The rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥ / al-mubāḥ.
